name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8, sold as Neutrazen, is a lab-made peptide used in products for sensitive, red or irritated skin. People use it to calm irritation and reduce visible redness so the complexion looks more even.

Suppliers describe it as dampening inflammatory signalling in skin, which means less visible redness and discomfort. It has been identified among peptides used in facial products for sensitive skin. Published research is laboratory work or tests of blended formulas, including its use as a targeting molecule for the melanocortin 1 receptor in liposome delivery; no standalone human trial was found.

paras: It is applied in leave-on creams and serums made for sensitive or redness-prone skin, usually as part of a gentle daily routine. Calming effects from such products are generally noticed over days to weeks.
Product labels advise a patch test and stopping use if irritation occurs. No specific adverse-effect literature was found.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8 (Neutrazen) is a soothing peptide used in products for sensitive or reddish skin, aimed at calmer, more even-looking skin. It is described as dampening skin inflammatory signals, which reduces visible redness. Published research is laboratory and multi-ingredient formula work.

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8, marketed as Neutrazen, is a synthetic lipopeptide used in cosmetics for sensitive or redness-prone skin. It is promoted as calming irritation-related redness and discomfort.

It has been identified among the peptides used in facial products for sensitive skin [1][2]. Published evidence on its own effects is limited to formulation and laboratory work, often in multi-ingredient products [3][4].
infobox: Cosmetic ingredient; appears in a US-listed topical mist label

paras: Surveys of cosmetic products labelled for sensitive skin catalogue synthetic peptides among their active ingredients [1][2]. Suppliers describe palmitoyl tripeptide-8 as an anti-inflammatory, soothing peptide. A US drug-label listing for a facial mist containing it directs users to mist it onto cleansed skin and advises a patch test, avoiding eye contact, and stopping use if irritation occurs [5].

No studies found. Related laboratory work includes a 2025 study that conjugated the peptide to liposomes to target melanocytes carrying the melanocortin 1 receptor for delivery of glabridin [3], and a 2025 laboratory study of a multi-ingredient dermatological base that contained it and reported effects on inflammatory and matrix-related markers [4]. These do not test the peptide alone in people.
